problems.location: Concept 1: Situated Learning Ecologies and Workplace Transfer / block 5
problems.lesson_text: Workplace training research indicates that environmental support and transfer climate exert the strongest influence on whether skills transfer to live contexts (Blume et al., 2010; Rouiller & Goldstein, 1993).
problems.source_text: They found that environmental support has the largest effect on transfer; organizational constraints also had a modest effect.
problems.reason: The source names environmental support alone as having the largest effect; it does not rank transfer climate as strongest.

problems.location: Concept 3: Cognitive Mechanisms of Retention: Retrieval, Spacing, and Interleaving / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Spacing intervals must match retention schedules; excessively long lags cause catastrophic forgetting, whereas massed cramming creates short-term fluency followed by steep decay.
problems.source_text: Cepeda and colleagues (2006) found that spaced practice led to greater recall than massed practice regardless of the size of the lag between practice and recall.
problems.reason: The source says spacing beat massing whatever the lag and only that wider spacing is "not necessarily always better", which contradicts the claim that long lags cause catastrophic forgetting.

problems.location: Concept 4: Generative Comprehension and Inferential Schema Building / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Typing often defaults to non-generative transcription; students require explicit guidance to distill rather than copy.
problems.source_text: Even when study participants using laptops were instructed to think about the information and type the notes in their own words, they were no better at synthesizing material than students who were not given the warning.
problems.reason: The source found that telling laptop typists to use their own words did not help, so the lesson's fix (explicit guidance) contradicts it.

problems.location: Concept 5: Achievement Goal Orientations, Self-Regulation, and Identity Threat / block 1
problems.lesson_text: While performance-approach goals can occasionally sustain short-term engagement and immediate rote recall, they often leave learners vulnerable to anxiety, task avoidance, and self-handicapping when difficulty spikes.
problems.source_text: These kinds of performance-avoidance goals have been associated with maladaptive learning behaviors including task avoidance (Middleton and Midgley, 1997; sixth-grade students), reduced effort (Elliot, 1999), and self-handicapping
problems.reason: After setting up approach and avoidance goals as separate, the lesson pins on approach goals the task avoidance and self-handicapping that the source links to avoidance goals.

problems.location: Concept 1: Situated Learning Ecologies and Workplace Transfer / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Relational, Community, Work-Based
problems.source_text: In Case C Case Aʼs course ... In Case C Case Bʼs platform ... The connections matter as much as any one source.
problems.reason: The slides show Case C as a whole ecosystem that includes Case A's course and Case B's platform, but the lesson casts Case C as a separate alternative that rivals the course and the platform.

problems.location: Concept 2: Pedagogical Functions and Ethical Trade-offs of Visible versus Invisible AI / block 4
problems.lesson_text: Although deployed for security or proctoring, persistent monitoring changes classroom psychological safety and erodes learner trust.
problems.source_text: None of the nine below is good or bad on its own. ... It can give peace of mind on one side of the screen. On the other side, it’s a record.
problems.reason: The source presents watching AI as two-sided and not good or bad on its own, but the lesson states as fact that it harms safety and trust.

problems.location: Concept 3: Cognitive Mechanisms of Retention: Retrieval, Spacing, and Interleaving / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Interleaving problem types dramatically enhances mathematical problem solving and category induction (Carvalho & Goldstone, 2014a; Rohrer et al., 2015).
problems.source_text: Several studies have shown benefits for blocking, at least for category learning ... interleaved study improves learning of highly similar categories (by facilitating between-category comparisons), whereas blocked study improves learning of low-similarity categories
problems.reason: The source presents mixed evidence where the best choice depends on the task, but the lesson presents interleaving as plainly better and leaves out the benefits of blocking.

problems.location: Concept 2: Pedagogical Functions and Ethical Trade-offs of Visible versus Invisible AI / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Rigid rubrics penalize non-standard creativity; reinforces historical bias
problems.source_text: Fast can be useful. But scoring wants neat categories, and one rubric for everybody leaves little room for the things that make a person interesting.
problems.reason: The Compass page does not say judging AI reinforces historical bias; the lesson adds this claim.

problems.location: Concept 2: Pedagogical Functions and Ethical Trade-offs of Visible versus Invisible AI / block 2

problems.source_text: It can give peace of mind on one side of the screen. On the other side, it’s a record. ... Try this: Ask your school what its monitoring software flags, who sees the list, and how long it’s kept.
problems.reason: The source says watching creates a record and asks how long it is kept; "chills intellectual exploration" and "permanent disciplinary records" are not in it.

problems.location: Concept 2: Pedagogical Functions and Ethical Trade-offs of Visible versus Invisible AI / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Kinesthetic learning; natural, voice-driven interaction
problems.source_text: When AI has a voice or a body, it feels less like software and more like a friend. That makes it intuitive, and easy to get attached to.
problems.reason: The source never presents embodied AI as an opportunity for kinesthetic learning.

problems.location: Concept 3: Cognitive Mechanisms of Retention: Retrieval, Spacing, and Interleaving / block 1
problems.lesson_text: Rereading and highlighting create an illusion of fluency because the perceptual representation is currently active in working memory; however, this passive familiarity fails to engage the neural mechanisms that secure long-term access.
problems.source_text: one possible reason why massed re-readings do not promote learning is that when people reread immediately, they do not attend to the most informative and meaningful portions of the material during the second reading
problems.reason: The source gives a different reason why rereading fails and never mentions an "illusion of fluency" or working-memory activation.

problems.location: Concept 5: Achievement Goal Orientations, Self-Regulation, and Identity Threat / block 4
problems.lesson_text: Their efficacy is heavily moderated by institutional context, teacher implementation fidelity, and the objective structural barriers present in the learning ecology. Brief psychological interventions cannot compensate for chronically under-resourced learning environments.

problems.reason: The source leaves open which conditions matter; the specific moderators and the claim about under-resourced settings are added by the lesson.
